props.title: Viva Las Vegas

sections.content: Viva Las Vegas represents peak Elvis Presley musical entertainment, pairing the King with the electrifying Ann-Margret in what became one of his most successful and energetic films. The chemistry between Elvis and Ann-Margret literally scorches the screen - their dance numbers, particularly the "C'mon Everybody" sequence, showcase two performers at the height of their physical and charismatic powers. Director George Sidney, who previously helmed Bye Bye Birdie (1963), brings his sharp eye for musical staging while capturing the neon-drenched excitement of 1960s Las Vegas before it became corporatized.

sections.content: The Las Vegas musical subgenre peaked in the early 1960s, with Viva Las Vegas arriving just as the city was transitioning from mob-run gambling town to entertainment capital. The Las Vegas Story (1952) had earlier portrayed the city as a film noir setting, while Meet Me in Las Vegas (1956) established the template for romantic musicals set against the casino backdrop. Elvis's film captured Vegas at a crucial turning point, before Howard Hughes began buying up casinos in 1966 and corporate ownership changed the Strip forever.

What makes Viva Las Vegas particularly significant is how it documents Elvis at his Hollywood peak, before his career decline and eventual 1969 Vegas comeback. The film's racing subplot may seem forced, but it provides the framework for some of Elvis's most dynamic musical numbers, including the title track which became one of his signature songs. Ann-Margret matches Elvis step-for-step, creating a partnership that influenced their later careers - she would go on to headline in Vegas for decades while Elvis became synonymous with the city during his 1970s residencies. sections.content: The portrayal of Las Vegas in cinema shifted dramatically after Viva Las Vegas. While Elvis's film showed a glamorous playground, later films like Leaving Las Vegas (1995) and Casino (1995) exposed darker undercurrents. Rain Man (1988) used Vegas as a backdrop for personal transformation, while Swingers (1996) captured the city's 1990s renaissance as a hip destination. Modern portrayals like Ocean's Eleven (2001) blend nostalgia for old Vegas with contemporary sophistication.
